title: Strategy Leadership Lab
text:
Content Overview
Strategy Leadership Lab is a weekly working session for the roughly 30 students who lead the BYU Strategy Program and the four career clubs it administers: MCA, PMA, CSA, and WSA. Those clubs serve students across campus by career interest rather than by major, and the leadership team reflects that: about half of the people in this room are majoring in something other than strategy. It exists to do two things at once: develop you as a leader, and give the whole leadership team protected time to coordinate on shared priorities.
The Lab is the primary coordination mechanism in the Strategy Program operating model. One meeting cadence governs the entire program.
Enrollment is limited to program and club leaders and is open to them regardless of major. It is optional but encouraged for everyone serving in a presidency. If your schedule prevents you from enrolling, you are welcome to audit or simply attend.

text:
Discussant
Once during the semester you lead the front of the room for fifteen minutes. The reading, quote, and scripture are assigned; you bring a leader profile, one question of your own, and the facilitation. Two or three discussants share each session, so everyone takes exactly one turn.
Your job is to run the discussion, not to summarize the reading. Three of the four questions are the same every week and are written for you; the fourth is yours, on anything you are curious about. If the discussants are the only ones talking, it has not worked.
Circulate a one-page brief on the reading by Tuesday 11:59 PM so the rest of the room can take part whether or not they finished it. The brief is graded with the turn.
Sign-ups happen in week one. Everyone gets one turn, so the fifteen minutes weigh the same for a paid co-president and an unpaid VP. Full detail, including how to run a discussion that does not die, is on the Being a Discussant page.
There is no separate AI assessment. AI proficiency is built and demonstrated in the weekly drills, which is why the paid subscription is required. See Required Tools in the syllabus.

title: Operating Model
text:
Strategy Program Operating Model
The Strategy Program administers four career clubs that serve students across campus. Club membership is open by career interest, not by major: a student headed for consulting, product, or corporate strategy belongs in the relevant club whether they are a strategy major or not. Roughly half the leaders in this room are majoring in something else.
The program has grown by 50% over the last five years and now serves 120 new students per year through the major, plus another 100 to 200 students from other majors across the Marriott School and campus. The operating model below aligns faculty, student leaders, career services, and academic advisement at that scale. It has three parts.

title: Session Template
text:
Session Template
Every session runs the same five blocks in the same order, the way a practice does. The sequence does not change week to week. What changes is the content inside each block.
The first three blocks are the 30 minute leadership development block. Practice is the 45 minute working block, published on the schedule as the project roundtable.

title: Session Template
text:
Announcements (5 min)
Program logistics only. Anything that takes longer than a minute to explain belongs in Practice or in email. Standing items:

Upcoming club events and who owns them
Deadlines landing this week or next
Recruiting calendar changes
New hires, role changes, vacancies

title: Session Template
text:
Discussant Block (15 min)
Student led, faculty curated. You assign the reading, the quote, and the scripture. Two or three discussants deliver them, add a leader profile of their own choosing, and run the discussion. Everyone takes one turn across the semester.
The reading carries the week’s leadership principle, drawn from the three skill areas the operating model names: influence, conflict, and managing up. Guest speakers and case discussions take this block on the weeks they appear.
Keep the quote, scripture, and profile to five minutes together. The quote and scripture are always a pair, both speaking to the same principle from two directions. The profile is three or four sentences: who they are, the decision worth knowing, what it cost them.
Run a discussion, do not give a presentation. Fifteen minutes split two or three ways is not enough to summarize a reading, and a summary is not what the block is for. Three standing questions carry every week, grounded in the golden mean: name the virtue, name where it becomes a vice, name when the quote stops applying. Discussants add a fourth of their own. If the discussants are the only ones talking, it has failed.
Discussants circulate a one-page brief by Tuesday 11:59 PM so someone who did not finish the reading can still take part.

title: Session Template
text:
Drills (10 min)
A follow-along. You are at the front with your screen up, everyone has a laptop open, and the room builds the same thing at the same time. Nobody watches a demo. If a student’s screen is dark, the drill is not working.
The default format is an AI follow-along: you narrate the prompt, everyone types their own version, and the interesting part is where the outputs differ. Ten minutes is enough for one artifact, not a workflow. Pick something a leader would actually produce this week.
Candidates:

Draft the recruiting email to a firm contact, then compare what six people got back
Turn a messy set of event notes into a one page brief
Build the agenda for a club presidency meeting from a two sentence description
Take a plan someone wrote and have AI argue against it, then judge whether it was right
Summarize a case or article into the three sentences you would say out loud

Rules that keep it a drill and not a lecture:

Everyone types. You go slow enough that the slowest person keeps up.
Same starting prompt for the room, so the differences are visible.
Stop at ten minutes even if it is unfinished. Unfinished is fine, it makes the point.
Two or three people read their output out loud before you move on.

If a follow-along needs more room, take the extra five minutes from Practice rather than from the Principle block.

title: Session Template
text:
Practice (45 min)
Students take the rest of the hour and actually do the work. The drill showed them the move once. Practice is where they run it on their own club’s real deliverable, at their own desk, for forty five minutes.
Scott, Sarah, and Luke roam the room the whole time. Roaming is the instruction method here. There is no front of the room during Practice.
What roaming looks like:

Read over a shoulder before saying anything
Ask what they are trying to do, not what they are doing
Two minutes per student, then move. Come back around rather than camping.
Carry patterns forward: if three people hit the same wall, stop the room and say so

Sarah and Luke have two modes and can pick per week:

In the room. Roam alongside Scott, same job, three coaches covering thirty students.
Broken out. Pull a subgroup into a side conversation: a club that needs focused help, a first-time VP who needs onboarding, a team with a deadline that week. Or run their own work while available to the room.

Decide the mode in prep, not on the fly, so the room knows who to look for.
Club and presidency updates and cross-team coordination still need a home. Either give them the first ten minutes of Practice before students scatter, or fold the standing items into Announcements. Pick one and keep it the same every week.

title: Weekly Updates
text:
Weekly Updates
Every student in the Lab sends a written end-of-week update to the person they report to, with strategy-program@byu.edu in CC.
That is the whole mechanism, and it is accountability all the way up the chain. A club VP reports to their co-presidents. Those co-presidents report to Soraya. The program co-presidents report to Scott. Nobody reports into a void, and nobody is left guessing what the people below them did this week.
The CC does two things: it gives the Strategy Program one place to track completion, and it means your leader is never the only person who knows you did the work.

title: Weekly Updates
text:
What Makes a Good Update

Short. Bullets, not paragraphs. If it runs past one screen, cut it.
Specific. Numbers, names, dates. “Good turnout” tells your leader nothing.
Honest about blockers. Flagging a problem early is the entire point. A clean update every week from a team that is struggling is worse than no update at all.
Consistent. The value is in the streak. Twelve on-time updates build a record of the semester that nobody has to reconstruct in December.

title: Feedback Conversations
text:
Feedback Conversations
Twice a semester you sit down with the person you report to and have a real conversation about how the work is going, in both directions. Then each of you submits a short reflection saying it happened and what you took from it.
There is no survey and no rating form. Filling out a scored questionnaire about someone you see every week is awkward, and it produces a document instead of a conversation. The conversation is the point. Learning to give a colleague a specific, useful, uncomfortable piece of feedback in person is the single most transferable skill in this course.

title: Feedback Conversations
text:
What Is Graded
The reflection, not the feedback. You get credit for having the conversation and submitting your reflection. Nothing anyone says about you affects your grade, in either direction.
That is deliberate. If the feedback you received moved your grade, everyone would learn to say pleasant things, and the instrument would be worth nothing. It also keeps the course fair across employees and volunteers: a conversation costs the same thirty minutes whether you are paid for nine hours a week or volunteering for four.

title: Feedback Conversations
text:
How the Conversation Goes
Thirty minutes, both directions. The leader goes first, then asks for feedback on their own leadership. A conversation where only one person hears anything is a performance review, not a feedback conversation.
Structure:

Strengths. What is working. Be specific enough that they know which behavior to keep.
One thing to work on. Not three. One, chosen because it would make the most difference.
Support. What you can do to help.
Turn it around. The person who spoke first now asks: what should I be doing differently?

The question to ask, in both directions: which way did I miss, too little or too much? Every principle has two failure modes, so “you were not courageous enough” and “you fought for ego” are different corrections. Directional is far easier to answer than a rating, and it is the only kind of answer you can act on. See Principles.

title: Feedback Conversations
text:
What to Talk About
Four dimensions, the same ones used across the strategy program. The Principles page is the other half of that vocabulary, and either one works as an agenda.
Ownership. Whether they drive the work.







Where they might be
What it looks like




Early
Waits to be told. Work stops when the next step is unclear. Blockers surface at the deadline


Solid
Owns a defined piece and finishes it. Raises blockers early. Still needs the plan handed to them


Strong
Owns their area end to end and pulls others along. Reprioritizes when things change, and what comes back is better than what was asked for



Collaboration. Whether people want them on their team.







Where they might be
What it looks like




Early
Works alone and the team finds out late. Takes feedback as criticism, or agrees and changes nothing


Solid
Reliable teammate. Reviews others’ work when asked, shares context, acts on feedback next time


Strong
Raises the standard of the whole team. Handles disagreement without it becoming personal, and changes position publicly when someone else is right



Communication. The artifacts: updates, emails, decks, announcements.







Where they might be
What it looks like




Early
Updates are late or absent. The reader has to ask what happened


Solid
Answer first, support underneath. Someone reading the first line knows the state of the work


Strong
Writes for the specific reader. Produces the thing the team reuses



Your twelve weekly updates are the evidence here. Pull them up during the conversation.
Stakeholder Presence. How they show up in front of someone senior or outside the club: recruiters, alumni, firm contacts, faculty, students from other majors.







Where they might be
What it looks like




Early
Avoids the contact. Silent, or speaks and creates confusion someone else repairs


Solid
Prepared and credible on their own work. Does not yet steer the conversation


Strong
The firm contact asks for this person by name. Surfaces a risk before anyone else finds it



Nobody is strong on all four. The useful conversation is about one of them.

title: Feedback Conversations
text:
The Reflection
Short. Four things, submitted by each person independently:

Who you met with and when
The one thing you are working on next
One thing you committed to as a result
One thing you asked them to do differently

Write about yourself, not about them. This is not a place to record what someone else is bad at. If something came up that needs more than a conversation, bring it to Scott, Soraya, or your faculty advisor directly. It does not travel through a reflection.

title: Being a Discussant
text:
Being a Discussant
Once during the semester you and one or two others own the front of the room for fifteen minutes.
The reading, the quote, and the scripture are assigned. You do not choose them. What you bring is the leader profile, one question of your own, and the ability to get twenty-six people talking.
Everyone takes exactly one turn. Twenty-seven leaders, twelve sessions, two or three discussants a week.

title: Being a Discussant
text:
The Job in One Sentence
Get twenty-six busy people to think out loud about one idea for ten minutes.
That is harder than presenting and it is a different skill. Presenting is something you can do alone in a room. Running a discussion means the other people have to talk, which means your preparation is mostly about them, not about you.

title: Being a Discussant
text:
What You Actually Do
Week one: sign up. Pick a session. The reading for each session is already assigned, so you are choosing a date and a topic together.
Two weeks out: meet your co-discussants. Fifteen minutes on a call is enough. Decide who takes the quote and scripture, who takes the leader profile, and who opens the discussion. Three of your questions are already written for you. Agree on the fourth.
One week out: read it properly. Not a skim. You need to know what the reading argues, what it gets wrong, and what it would mean for someone running a club at BYU. Bring an opinion.
Tuesday, 11:59 PM: circulate the brief. One page, to the whole class. See below.
Friday, 12:35: run it.

title: Being a Discussant
text:
The One-Page Brief
One page. Not two. Sent to the class by Tuesday 11:59 PM so people have three days.
Five parts:

The quote and the scripture, printed, and what you think they share
The reading, with a link and an honest time estimate
What it argues, in three or four sentences
Why it matters here. One paragraph connecting it to something a club leader in this program actually faces
Your own question, the fourth one. Anything you are curious about. Printed, so people can think about it before Friday

The brief exists so that someone who did not finish the reading can still take part. That is not a loophole, it is the design. Twenty-seven club leaders in October will not all finish every reading, and a discussion that only works if everyone did is a discussion that fails half the time.

title: Being a Discussant
text:
The Fifteen Minutes



Minutes
What




3
Quote and scripture


2
Leader profile


10
Discussion



The quote and the scripture. Assigned, always as a pair, both speaking to the week’s principle from two directions.
Your job is not to find them, it is to land them. Read both out loud, say in one sentence what you think they share, and stop. Do not explain either for two minutes.
Sometimes the pair will not say the identical thing. A quote about decisiveness beside a scripture about patience is not a mistake; it is the mean, put in the room before anyone has argued about it. If you notice the tension, say so. That is usually the best sentence anyone says in the first three minutes.
The leader profile. This one is yours to choose. Three or four sentences: who they are, the decision or moment worth knowing, what it cost them. A real person, living or dead, ideally one nobody in the room would have picked. Pick someone who fits the week’s principle, including someone who got it wrong.
The discussion. Open with a question, not a summary. Everyone read the brief; they do not need you to recap it.

title: Being a Discussant
text:
The Three Standing Questions
Every discussion in this course asks the same three questions. They do not change week to week, and you do not have to invent them.

What about this leader or this reading inspires you? Name the principle. Not “they were great,” but which specific quality, and what it looked like in practice. The Principles page has fourteen to choose from.
Where does that principle become a vice? Push it too far and every strength turns into something else. Name what it becomes, and if you can, name a time you have seen the excess in this program.
Under what conditions does the quote stop applying? When would you have acted differently than this leader did, and why?

Then bring one question of your own. Anything you are curious about: something in the reading, something it made you think about, something happening in the program right now. Three questions are standardized so you are not starting from a blank page. The fourth is yours.
You will not get through all four in ten minutes. That is expected. Two good ones beat four rushed ones.

title: Being a Discussant
text:
Why These Three Questions
They come from the golden mean, the framework the Principles page lays out.
Aristotle argued that a virtue is not a feeling or a single act but a settled disposition to choose well, and that it sits in a mean between two failure modes: one of doing too little and one of doing too much. Courage is not the opposite of cowardice; it sits between cowardice and recklessness. There are two ways to miss, not one.
That is why leadership advice so often contradicts itself. “Be decisive” and “gather input” are not opposing camps, they are the two ways of missing the same mean. A co-president who never decides is halting. One who decides before anyone has spoken is impulsive. The question is never which advice is right, it is where the mean sits for this decision, this week, with these people.
Most leadership quotes are a maximum dressed up as a truth. Question 2 is how you find the edge, and question 3 is how you find the conditions where the edge matters.
Use the principles table. Naming the principle is the whole first move, and “what is the excess version of this” is much easier to answer once it has a name. All fourteen are on the Principles page with both failure modes already written.

title: Being a Discussant
text:
How to Run a Discussion
Six things that decide whether this works:
Open with your hardest question, not your easiest. A warm-up question gets warm-up answers and you have ten minutes.
Make the fourth one arguable. The three standing questions already are. “What did you think of the reading?” produces silence. “The author says you should never escalate to your advisor without telling your co-president first. When is that wrong?” produces an argument. Ask what you actually want to know, not what sounds like a discussion question.
Count to ten in your head. The silence after a question feels much longer to you than to anyone else. Almost every discussion that dies is killed by the facilitator answering their own question at second four.
Call on people by name. You know all twenty-six of them. Use it. “You ran the case workshop last week, does this match what happened?” beats asking the room in general.
Do not answer your own questions. Your opinion is the least useful one in the room during your fifteen minutes.
Follow the fire. If the room catches on question one, ride it and drop the rest. Getting through all four is not the goal.

title: Being a Discussant
text:
Grading
Fifteen points, 15% of the course grade.








Points




Brief circulated on time, one page, five parts present
5


Your fourth question is a real question, one you actually want answered
5


You ran a discussion rather than gave a presentation
5



The third one is the whole point. If you and your co-discussants did most of the talking, that is the section that loses points, no matter how well prepared you were.

title: Being a Discussant
section: If You Cannot Make Your Week
text:
If You Cannot Make Your Week
Swap with someone. Arrange it in advance and tell Scott. Do not spend your free absence on the one session where twenty-six people are counting on you.

title: Principles
text:
Principles
These are the principles of the strategy program. The same fourteen apply across the program’s courses and clubs, here applied to running a club.
Each principle carries a scripture reference, collected at the end of this page.
The sources they draw on, following Brigham Young’s admonition to gather up all the good and true principles wherever we find them: the BYU Marriott mission and values, the standard works, Christlike Attributes from Preach My Gospel, Amazon’s leadership principles, Bridgewater’s original philosophy, McKinsey’s purpose, mission and values, John Wooden’s Pyramid of Success, and Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics, Book II.

title: Principles
section: Why They Are Written This Way
text:
Why They Are Written This Way
Most codes of conduct list principles to be maximized: be excellent, be truthful, be bold. Stated that way they have two problems.
The first is that almost any good quality can be taken to excess. Truthfulness can overshoot into cruelty. Excellence can overshoot into perfectionism, or into standards that humiliate people. Initiative can overshoot into recklessness. A list of maxims gives you no way to say “you are doing too much of a good thing,” so the only correction on offer is to abandon the principle, which nobody wants.
The second is that two good principles collide. Speed collides with rigor. Candor collides with charity. Excellence collides with a deadline.
Aristotle solved both with the golden mean. Every good quality of character sits between two failure modes, one of doing too little and one of doing too much. Courage is not the opposite of cowardice; it sits between cowardice and recklessness. Generosity sits between stinginess and waste. The failure is never the quality itself. It is having too little or too much of it, at the wrong moment, toward the wrong person, for the wrong reason.
The mean is not fixed by a formula. It is found by judgment, and judgment is built by practice. Each principle below is written with both of its failures named, because you cannot aim for the mean if you do not know the extremes.
These are aspirational. Everyone misses, often, in both directions. We keep striving, and over time develop true wisdom.

Success is peace of mind which is a direct result of self-satisfaction in knowing you made the effort to become the best of which you are capable.
John Wooden

title: Principles
section: For Some Things There Is No Golden Mean
text:
For Some Things There Is No Golden Mean
Almost everything above is a matter of degree. A few things are not. Aristotle is explicit that the doctrine has limits: some acts “imply by their names that they are themselves bad,” and of those “it is not possible, then, ever to be right with regard to them.” There is no correct amount of them, so they are not on the scale.

title: Principles
text:
When Principles Collide
They will. Rigor says check it again; the deadline says ship. Courage says say it now; discernment says not in this room, not in front of these people. Excellence says raise the bar; patience says this is not the week.
There is no rule that decides. Aristotle says the judgment “rests with perception,” meaning the read of a person who is actually present and has done this before. That is why the answer to a hard call is usually a conversation rather than a lookup.
Three practical aids.
Name the collision out loud. “I think rigor and the deadline are fighting here” is a faster route to a decision than arguing the merits as though only one principle were in play.
Correct against your own pull. Aiming straight at the mean undershoots, because your own habit is already bending you. Learn which way you personally miss, then overcorrect. “We shall get into the intermediate state by drawing well away from error, as people do in straightening sticks that are bent.”
The red face test. When a situation is genuinely ambiguous, ask whether you could explain the decision to a respected leader without being red in the face. If not, do not do it.

title: Principles
text:
Which Way Did I Miss?
The most useful question you can ask a peer, given how this page is written, is directional: which way did I miss, too little or too much?
That is far easier for a teammate to answer than a rating, and it is the only kind of answer you can act on. Use it in your feedback conversations, and use it after any meeting or event you ran.
